### HW-8: Two cores, and which one is running
- Fact: The chip has two cores. The special register `cnum` reads the
  number of the core executing (0 or 1).
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/cpu.h` line 43
  (`CPU_CORE_NUM 2`) and line 82 (`cnum`); SDK `csfr.h` line 245 (`CNUM`);
  E-4: `cnum` read 0 on core 0 and 1 on core 1.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-4)
- Needed by: M0d

### HW-9: Releasing core 1
- Fact: Core 1 does not run until core 0 releases it. To release it, put
  core 1's start address in the word at `0x01C7FFF8`, then set bit 3 of
  `C1_CON` (`0x01EEE004`, the second word of the `corex2` block at
  `0x01EEE000`). Core 1 then starts at the address in that word and runs
  alongside core 0. That word is also the vector table's slot for source
  126 (software interrupt 6, HW-18): don't use software interrupt 6 while
  the word holds core 1's start address, and don't overwrite the word
  before core 1 has started.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 41, 106-112 (`C1_CON`); SDK `hwi.h`
  lines 114-123 (source 126 is `0x01C7FE00 + 4 × 126` = `0x01C7FFF8`); RE
  `docs/io/01-boot.md` §1 (the word at `0x01C7FFF8` holds core 1's start
  address) and §5.2 (bit 3 of `C1_CON`); E-4: with the entry in that word,
  setting `C1_CON` bit 3 started core 1 there.
- Standing: confirmed (RE, E-4)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-10: Core 1's state when it starts, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, core 1 starts in supervisor mode, and its start address
  must be in the code window or in RAM. Its stack pointers hold values the
  firmware must not rely on: core 1's first instructions set its own `sp`
  (and `ssp`, `usp` if it will use them). fwtest releases core 1 once;
  later writes do not restart it. Warning: fwtest also releases core 1 when
  bit 3 of `JL_CLOCK->SYS_DIV` (`0x00010008`) goes from 0 to 1, so leave
  that bit alone unless releasing core 1 is meant; use `C1_CON` (HW-9).
  Whether a raw image on the chip can rely on the same release is part of
  Q-11.
- Sources: the emulator model; E-4 (core 1 ran on stacks it set itself).
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M1

### HW-11: The clocks
- Fact: On the chip, the board's reference crystal is 24 MHz. In fwtest
  the clock is fixed: each core executes one instruction per cycle at
  240 MHz (240 000 cycles an emulated millisecond) from the start, writes
  to the clock registers have no effect, and no clock set-up is needed. How
  to set the clocks up on the chip, and which system clock rates it
  supports, is open (Q-2).
- Sources: RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §5.2 (the reference clock detected is
  24 MHz on the FM-1); HARNESS ("Time": 240 000 cycles a millisecond, one
  instruction of core 0 a cycle); the emulator model (core 1 at the same
  rate, the clock registers).
- Standing: confirmed (RE)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-50: EMU_CON and EMU_MSG, per core
- Fact: Each core has `EMU_CON`, `EMU_MSG`, `EMU_SSP_H`, `EMU_SSP_L`,
  `EMU_USP_H` and `EMU_USP_L`: core 0's at `0x01EEF0D0`, `0x01EEF0D4`,
  `0x01EEF0D8`, `0x01EEF0DC`, `0x01EEF0E0`, `0x01EEF0E4`, core 1's `0x200`
  higher. `EMU_MSG` says which core-level condition raised the exception,
  one bit each: bit 0 misaligned access, bit 1 illegal instruction, bit 2
  division by zero, bit 3 stack overflow, bit 8 watchpoint 0, bits 16 to
  20 floating point invalid, infinite, tiny, huge, inexact. The SDK clears
  it by writing all ones. `EMU_CON` bit 3 turns on the stack check against
  `EMU_SSP_L` and `EMU_SSP_H` (the SDK's values: the bottom and top of the
  supervisor stack) and `EMU_USP_L` and `EMU_USP_H` (the SDK's values: 0
  and `0xFFFFFFFF`, no user-stack check). The SDK also sets `EMU_CON`
  bits 2 and 8. That `EMU_CON` bit n turns on the
  condition of `EMU_MSG` bit n is suggested by these settings but not
  stated (Q-14).
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214 (one `q32DSP` block per core from
  `0x01EEF000`, `0x200` apart) and 267-272 (the six words, 0x34 to 0x39);
  SDK `cpu/wl82/debug.c` lines 70-110 (the bit names), 1098-1099 (the
  clear), 1113-1117 and 1164-1169 (bit 3 and the limits), 1193 (bits 2 and
  8); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §5.2 (FM-1's own firmware programs these
  registers).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-51: DBG_MSG on the chip reports exception causes
- **Q-10. Interrupt details on the chip.** Whether the chip switches
  stacks on an interrupt from user mode exactly as HW-3 says; its nesting
  rules and choice among pending sources (HW-22); whether the two cores
  share one vector table; what `idle` does with interrupts masked (HW-24).
  The toolchain's interrupt attribute works in fwtest.
- **Q-11. Booting on the chip.** The contents of the boot-parameter block
  the loader passes in r0, and whether a raw image can be started on real
  hardware without M-VAVE's loader (PLAN.md, M9 risk), and whether such an
  image can release core 1 as HW-9 says.
- **Q-12. MIDI input.** UART1 and the MIDI jack are not covered here (M6
  will ask).
- **Q-13. The timer acknowledge on the chip.** Whether writing a TIMER0-3
  `CON` to acknowledge its interrupt restarts the count, as it does in
  fwtest (HW-48), or the count runs on and the period stays `PRD` counts.
  The SDK's examples acknowledge every interrupt with such a write but
  don't say. Settled by a probe on real hardware.
- **Q-14. CPU exceptions on the chip.** What the sources don't establish
  about source 1 (HW-49 to HW-51): which causes are on when an installed
  app starts, and which `EMU_CON` and `DBG_EN` bits turn each on (the SDK's
  settings suggest bit n for cause n, but its demonstration reports a
  misaligned access although the SDK never sets `EMU_CON` bit 0); whether
  the exception obeys the source's `ICFG` enable, `icfg` bit 8 and `sti`
  like other sources; what `reti` holds (the faulting instruction or the
  next) and whether the faulting access or division completes; how the
  stack limits are compared; whether an undecodable instruction raises it
  (`EMU_MSG` bit 1 is named "illegal instruction"); whether a write to the
  code window does. fwtest models none of it (HW-52). Settled by a probe on
  real hardware.
- **Q-15. SPI1's interrupt on the chip.** Whether source 16 follows the
  pending flag and `CON` bit 13 together (so setting bit 13 while a
  finished transfer is still pending raises it at once, and clearing bit
  13 withdraws it), or only a transfer that finishes while bit 13 is set
  raises it, as in fwtest (HW-59). The SDK's example sets bit 13 before
  it starts a transfer and acknowledges in the handler, which works either
  way. Settled by a probe on real hardware.

# Toolchain and SDK

## JieLi Linux toolchain (PROVENANCE P-1)

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Name | `jieli-linux-toolchains-20250324.1` |
| Published at | `https://pkgman.jieliapp.com/s/linux-toolchain` (vendor short link) |
| Pinned URL | `https://jl-update.oss-cn-shenzhen.aliyuncs.com/jieli-linux-toolchains-20250324.1.tar.xz` |
| Size | 26,009,040 bytes |
| SHA-256 | `f686586bcfb45e0f0bb27fd2b39c7a7f313cb4f0e88a66a14da621ffa8225958` |
| MD5 (server ETag) | `22a619513462abfc4d86ed50b2922ef7` |
| Server Last-Modified | Mon, 24 Mar 2025 02:39:21 GMT |
| Downloaded | 2026-10-21 |
| Contents | Clang/LLVM 4.0.1 with a pi32v2 backend; GNU Binutils ld 2.26.51.20160621 (targets `elf32-pi32v2`); Linux x86-64 binaries |

**The short link has moved on.** On 2026-10-21 the short link redirected to
`jieli-linux-toolchains-20260730.1.tar.xz` (a newer release), not the pinned
20250324.1. The pinned file is still served at its direct URL, which is what
`tools/Dockerfile` uses. Moving to a newer toolchain is a deliberate change
in its own pull request, with a new SHA-256 here.

### How it is used

- `tools/Dockerfile` downloads the pinned URL, checks the SHA-256 above
  (`sha256sum -c`; the build fails on any mismatch), and unpacks only
  `common/` and `pi32v2/` into `/opt/jieli` in a locally built image.
- The archive and the image are **never committed or published**: not in this
  repository, not in releases, and not pushed to any registry. CI builds the
  image fresh every run. `.gitignore` excludes `*.tar.xz`, and check
  C-NO-TOOLCHAIN fails if any tracked file looks like part of the toolchain.
- We compile with `clang -target pi32v2 -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib`
  and link with the toolchain's `ld`. We never link the toolchain's C library
  or its other runtime libraries (R-BUILD-1).

### Licence and terms files found inside

The archive has 695 entries. A search of every path for licence, copying,
notice, terms, EULA, readme and copyright found one file:

- `README.md` (Chinese, about 20 lines): usage notes only. After unpacking
  there are `common/`, `pi32/`, `pi32v2/` and `q32s/` directories; each chip
  family's tools are in its own directory, so set `CC` and similar variables
  in the Makefile; raise the open-file limit (`ulimit -n 8192`) before
  linking, or `ld` may fail with "File format not recognized". **No licence,
  copyright or terms of use.**

No other licence or terms file is present. The toolchain's licence terms are
therefore **unknown**, which is why we never redistribute it. It contains
components normally released under open licences (LLVM/Clang, GNU Binutils,
a newlib C library: `include/newlib.h` and libraries), but the archive
carries none of their licence texts.

### Compiler builtins

#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Vendors the parts of JieLi's AC79 SDK we use, from a pinned commit, and
# checks every file against vendor/jieli-sdk/SHA256SUMS (PROVENANCE P-2).
#
#   tools/fetch-sdk.sh --verify   check the committed files (default, offline)
#   tools/fetch-sdk.sh --fetch    re-download them from the pinned commit into
#                                 vendor/jieli-sdk/, then verify
#
# To vendor another file: add its path to SDK_FILES, run --fetch, add its
# hash to SHA256SUMS in the same commit, and log it in PROVENANCE.md.
set -eu

SDK_URL=https://gitee.com/Jieli-Tech/fw-AC79_AIoT_SDK.git
SDK_COMMIT=5fa84a9b2f723a5e9337ad79dc2ad741fc98fe2d
SDK_FILES="
LICENSE
include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/WL82.h
include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/csfr.h
"

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
DEST="$ROOT/vendor/jieli-sdk"
SUMS="$DEST/SHA256SUMS"

sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}

verify() {
    status=0
    # Every listed file must exist with the recorded hash...

**The short link has moved on.** On 2026-10-21 the short link redirected to
`jieli-linux-toolchains-20260730.1.tar.xz` (a newer release), not the pinned
20250324.1. The pinned file is still served at its direct URL, which is what
`tools/Dockerfile` uses. Moving to a newer toolchain is a deliberate change
in its own pull request, with a new SHA-256 here.

### How it is used

- `tools/Dockerfile` downloads the pinned URL, checks the SHA-256 above
  (`sha256sum -c`; the build fails on any mismatch), and unpacks only
  `common/` and `pi32v2/` into `/opt/jieli` in a locally built image.
- The archive and the image are **never committed or published**: not in this
  repository, not in releases, and not pushed to any registry. CI builds the
  image fresh every run. `.gitignore` excludes `*.tar.xz`, and check
  C-NO-TOOLCHAIN fails if any tracked file looks like part of the toolchain.
- We compile with `clang -target pi32v2 -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib`
  and link with the toolchain's `ld`. We never link the toolchain's C library
  or its other runtime libraries (R-BUILD-1).

### Licence and terms files found inside

The archive has 695 entries. A search of every path for licence, copying,
notice, terms, EULA, readme and copyright found one file:

- `README.md` (Chinese, about 20 lines): usage notes only. After unpacking
  there are `common/`, `pi32/`, `pi32v2/` and `q32s/` directories; each chip
  family's tools are in its own directory, so set `CC` and similar variables
  in the Makefile; raise the open-file limit (`ulimit -n 8192`) before
  linking, or `ld` may fail with "File format not recognized". **No licence,
  copyright or terms of use.**

No other licence or terms file is present. The toolchain's licence terms are
therefore **unknown**, which is why we never redistribute it. It contains
components normally released under open licences (LLVM/Clang, GNU Binutils,
a newlib C library: `include/newlib.h` and libraries), but the archive
carries none of their licence texts.

    list takes off 3 terms). So #61 passes once this pull request has
    merged and #61 has merged main.
- Answered: 2026-10-23, session SR-4-6 (spec side)

#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Builds the spec-side experiments (README.md) with the pinned toolchain
# container (tools/build.sh image) and writes SHA256SUMS.
#
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh            build into this folder
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh --check    build into a temporary folder
#                                                and compare with the committed
#                                                images (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS)
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh inside OUT (runs inside the container)
set -eu

HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
ROOT=$(cd "$HERE/../.." && pwd)
IMAGES="e2-console e3-timers e4-core1 e5-lcd e6-matrix e7-leds e8-adc e9-audio e10-faults e11-undefined e12-badjump e13-timer-ack e14-undefined-inline e15-spi1-irq e16-lcd-frame e17-adc-irq"

inside() {
    out=$1
    cd "$HERE"
    flags="-target pi32v2 -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror"
    clang -target pi32v2 -c start.S -o "$out/start.o"
    clang -target pi32v2 -c boot.S -o "$out/boot.o"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    clang $flags -c e1-boot.c -o "$out/e1-boot.o"
    ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/e1-boot.elf" "$out/boot.o" "$out/e1-boot.o"
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/e1-boot.elf" "$out/e1-boot.bin"
    for n in $IMAGES; do
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        clang $flags -c "$n.c" -o "$out/$n.o"
        ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/$n.elf" "$out/start.o" "$out/$n.o"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.bin"
    done
    rm -f "$out"/*.o "$out"/*.elf
    (cd "$out" && for n in e1-boot $IMAGES; do sha256sum "$n.bin"; done > SHA256SUMS)
}

build() {
    out=$1
<!--

# Spec-side black-box experiments (spec side only)

Small images the spec side runs in fwtest to confirm facts in
`docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (M0c). The spec cites them only as E-n and their
result; nothing here leaves `harness/`. They are written from the JieLi
SDK's register map and, where the SDK has no bit meanings, from the vendored
emulator's model (`exp.h` says which). Each confirms how fwtest presents the
board, not how real hardware behaves.

- Build: `sh harness/spec-experiments/build.sh` (the pinned toolchain
  container; writes `images/` and `images/SHA256SUMS`).
- Run: `sh harness/spec-experiments/run.sh OUT` rebuilds, compares with the
  committed images, and runs `experiments.suite` against this checkout's
  fwtest (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS, R-SPEC-4). The golden files are the results.
- Not part of fwtest: `harness/ci.sh` leaves this folder out of the fwtest
  build context, and the image-publishing workflow ignores it.

| ID | Image | What it shows (the golden files hold the numbers) |
|----|-------|---------------------------------------------------|
| E-1 | `e1-boot` | At entry: r0 = 0x01C7FC00, r2..r15, sp, usp, ssp, icfg, psr and cnum all 0 (r1 not observable: used as the pointer). The block at r0: first word 0x01C7FC40, the other 15 zero. The code window past the image reads 0xFFFFFFFF (erased flash), also 4 KiB further. A written word reads back at 0x01C7FDFC, 0x01CFFFFC, 0x01F3FFFC and 0x0407FFFC. |
| E-2 | `e2-console` | Word writes to DBG_MSG append their 4 bytes, low byte first. A byte or halfword write appends 4 bytes too: the written bytes merged into the last word written (console "abcd12:\nX2:\nYZ:\nend\n"). |
| E-3 | `e3-timers` | TIMER5 PRD 600: an interrupt (63) every 100 µs; TIMER4 advanced 2400 counts (24 MHz) between two. TIMER0 prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: an interrupt (4) every 1 ms; its CON read in the handler is 0x8021 (bit 15 pending). TTMR with PRD 1234: an interrupt (3) every 10 ms. ILAT_SET bit 0: interrupt 120 once. Counts at 52.3 ms (the capture came late, below): 523, 52, 5, 1. |
| E-4 | `e4-core1` | With core 1's entry in the word at 0x01C7FFF8, setting C1_CON bit 3 starts core 1 there; cnum reads 0 on core 0 and 1 on core 1; core 1 ran on stacks it set itself. |
| E-5 | `e5-lcd` | SPI1 bytes with PC8 low are commands, high data. CASET/RASET/RAMWR with RGB565 pixels high byte first, by single bytes (BUF) and by DMA (ADR, CNT from RAM) both draw. INVON and DISPOFF leave the captured picture as written. A software reset (0x01) clears it to black. |
| E-6 | `e6-matrix` | The log gives each fwtest key's (column, row) and each encoder's two contacts and their order (clockwise: the second contact closes first). Matches the table in the spec. |
| E-7 | `e7-leds` | LED line PA9, PA10, PH6, PH9 lights, in the selected column, the LED of the key at row 1, 2, 3, 4 of that column. |
| E-8 | `e8-adc` | Channel 4 reads the pot (900 at the start, then the script's 300, 0, 1023); channel 3 reads 640; every other channel 512. |
| E-9 | `e9-audio` | A half of 128 words (64 frames) every 1.451 ms after the first at 1.459 ms (44 117.6 frames a second). The first half to finish is half 0; the half just finished is CON0 bit 15 inverted. A sample is the word shifted right by 8, clamped to 16 bits: 0x007fffff gives 32767, 0xff800000 -32768, 0x01000000 32767, 0x00000080 0. |
| E-10 | `e10-faults` | No fault reaches sources 0-2 (handlers count 0), before and after writing EMU_CON 0x001F010F, EMU_SSP/USP limits excluding the stacks, DBG_EN 0x003F0030. Misaligned word loads give the bytes at the address (RAM+1: 0x04030201; code+1: 0x14131211); halfword loads at RAM+1 and +3 give 0x0100 and 0x0302 (the lowest address bit ignored); a word stored at RAM+9 lands in bytes 9-12. The addresses come from a volatile word: with constant addresses the compiler split the RAM accesses into byte accesses. Unmapped 0x00ABCDEC reads 0, and after a write still 0. A code-window write reads back unchanged. Signed and unsigned 1234/0 give 0; 1234%0 (as compiled) gives 1234. EMU_CON and the limits read back; EMU_MSG 0; DBG_EN 0 (unmodelled). The console is "E10\nend\n": writes to DBG_WR_EN and DBG_MSG_CLR between the two words left it alone. |
| E-11 | `e11-undefined` | A call to a function whose first halfword is 0xFFFF: the run ends as a fault ("cannot decode"), after the marker, with no handler run. |
| E-12 | `e12-badjump` | A call to 0x00ABCDEE: fwtest runs the zeros it reads there for 1024 instructions, then ends the run as a fault ("the pc left every memory"); no handler ran. |
| E-13 | `e13-timer-ack` | TIMER0, prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: 100 periods are 2 400 100 TIMER4 ticks with the acknowledge first in the handler (1 tick after entry) and 2 408 160 with it 82 ticks after entry; CNT reads 5 just before the acknowledge, 0 just after. The periphery model restarts the count and the period at every CON write. |
| E-14 | `e14-undefined-inline` | A marker store, then the halfword 0xFFFF in the same straight-line code: the run ends as a fault at the start of that code (the pc of main's first instruction), and the marker was never written. |
| E-15 | `e15-spi1-irq` | SPI1 CON bit 13 and source 16. CON reads 0x8000 before any write. Bit 13 never set, or written clear: no interrupt for a 2-byte DMA or a BUF byte. Bit 13 set: one interrupt each (the handler acknowledges with `CON |= 0x4000`); CON reads 0xA000. A DMA done with bit 13 set and the source off in ICFG, then CON written 0 and the source turned on: taken once. Before the SR-3 fix (vendor patch 0002, fwtest 0.2.0) a CON write could not clear bit 13, so the clear steps counted too. |
| E-16 | `e16-lcd-frame` | One CNT write of 115 200 bytes from RAM draws a whole frame (rows 0-119 red, 120-239 blue), pixel (0,0) green and (239,239) white in place. |

# Spec-side black-box experiments (spec side only)

Small images the spec side runs in fwtest to confirm facts in
`docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (M0c). The spec cites them only as E-n and their
result; nothing here leaves `harness/`. They are written from the JieLi
SDK's register map and, where the SDK has no bit meanings, from the vendored
emulator's model (`exp.h` says which). Each confirms how fwtest presents the
board, not how real hardware behaves.

- Build: `sh harness/spec-experiments/build.sh` (the pinned toolchain
  container; writes `images/` and `images/SHA256SUMS`).
- Run: `sh harness/spec-experiments/run.sh OUT` rebuilds, compares with the
  committed images, and runs `experiments.suite` against this checkout's
  fwtest (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS, R-SPEC-4). The golden files are the results.
- Not part of fwtest: `harness/ci.sh` leaves this folder out of the fwtest
  build context, and the image-publishing workflow ignores it.

| ID | Image | What it shows (the golden files hold the numbers) |
|----|-------|---------------------------------------------------|
| E-1 | `e1-boot` | At entry: r0 = 0x01C7FC00, r2..r15, sp, usp, ssp, icfg, psr and cnum all 0 (r1 not observable: used as the pointer). The block at r0: first word 0x01C7FC40, the other 15 zero. The code window past the image reads 0xFFFFFFFF (erased flash), also 4 KiB further. A written word reads back at 0x01C7FDFC, 0x01CFFFFC, 0x01F3FFFC and 0x0407FFFC. |
| E-2 | `e2-console` | Word writes to DBG_MSG append their 4 bytes, low byte first. A byte or halfword write appends 4 bytes too: the written bytes merged into the last word written (console "abcd12:\nX2:\nYZ:\nend\n"). |
| E-3 | `e3-timers` | TIMER5 PRD 600: an interrupt (63) every 100 µs; TIMER4 advanced 2400 counts (24 MHz) between two. TIMER0 prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: an interrupt (4) every 1 ms; its CON read in the handler is 0x8021 (bit 15 pending). TTMR with PRD 1234: an interrupt (3) every 10 ms. ILAT_SET bit 0: interrupt 120 once. Counts at 52.3 ms (the capture came late, below): 523, 52, 5, 1. |
| E-4 | `e4-core1` | With core 1's entry in the word at 0x01C7FFF8, setting C1_CON bit 3 starts core 1 there; cnum reads 0 on core 0 and 1 on core 1; core 1 ran on stacks it set itself. |
| E-5 | `e5-lcd` | SPI1 bytes with PC8 low are commands, high data. CASET/RASET/RAMWR with RGB565 pixels high byte first, by single bytes (BUF) and by DMA (ADR, CNT from RAM) both draw. INVON and DISPOFF leave the captured picture as written. A software reset (0x01) clears it to black. |
| E-6 | `e6-matrix` | The log gives each fwtest key's (column, row) and each encoder's two contacts and their order (clockwise: the second contact closes first). Matches the table in the spec. |
| E-7 | `e7-leds` | LED line PA9, PA10, PH6, PH9 lights, in the selected column, the LED of the key at row 1, 2, 3, 4 of that column. |
| E-8 | `e8-adc` | Channel 4 reads the pot (900 at the start, then the script's 300, 0, 1023); channel 3 reads 640; every other channel 512. |
| E-9 | `e9-audio` | A half of 128 words (64 frames) every 1.451 ms after the first at 1.459 ms (44 117.6 frames a second). The first half to finish is half 0; the half just finished is CON0 bit 15 inverted. A sample is the word shifted right by 8, clamped to 16 bits: 0x007fffff gives 32767, 0xff800000 -32768, 0x01000000 32767, 0x00000080 0. |
| E-10 | `e10-faults` | No fault reaches sources 0-2 (handlers count 0), before and after writing EMU_CON 0x001F010F, EMU_SSP/USP limits excluding the stacks, DBG_EN 0x003F0030. Misaligned word loads give the bytes at the address (RAM+1: 0x04030201; code+1: 0x14131211); halfword loads at RAM+1 and +3 give 0x0100 and 0x0302 (the lowest address bit ignored); a word stored at RAM+9 lands in bytes 9-12. The addresses come from a volatile word: with constant addresses the compiler split the RAM accesses into byte accesses. Unmapped 0x00ABCDEC reads 0, and after a write still 0. A code-window write reads back unchanged. Signed and unsigned 1234/0 give 0; 1234%0 (as compiled) gives 1234. EMU_CON and the limits read back; EMU_MSG 0; DBG_EN 0 (unmodelled). The console is "E10\nend\n": writes to DBG_WR_EN and DBG_MSG_CLR between the two words left it alone. |
| E-11 | `e11-undefined` | A call to a function whose first halfword is 0xFFFF: the run ends as a fault ("cannot decode"), after the marker, with no handler run. |
| E-12 | `e12-badjump` | A call to 0x00ABCDEE: fwtest runs the zeros it reads there for 1024 instructions, then ends the run as a fault ("the pc left every memory"); no handler ran. |
| E-13 | `e13-timer-ack` | TIMER0, prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: 100 periods are 2 400 100 TIMER4 ticks with the acknowledge first in the handler (1 tick after entry) and 2 408 160 with it 82 ticks after entry; CNT reads 5 just before the acknowledge, 0 just after. The periphery model restarts the count and the period at every CON write. |
| E-14 | `e14-undefined-inline` | A marker store, then the halfword 0xFFFF in the same straight-line code: the run ends as a fault at the start of that code (the pc of main's first instruction), and the marker was never written. |
| E-15 | `e15-spi1-irq` | SPI1 CON bit 13 and source 16. CON reads 0x8000 before any write. Bit 13 never set, or written clear: no interrupt for a 2-byte DMA or a BUF byte. Bit 13 set: one interrupt each (the handler acknowledges with `CON |= 0x4000`); CON reads 0xA000. A DMA done with bit 13 set and the source off in ICFG, then CON written 0 and the source turned on: taken once. Before the SR-3 fix (vendor patch 0002, fwtest 0.2.0) a CON write could not clear bit 13, so the clear steps counted too. |
| E-16 | `e16-lcd-frame` | One CNT write of 115 200 bytes from RAM draws a whole frame (rows 0-119 red, 120-239 blue), pixel (0,0) green and (239,239) white in place. |

### HW-53: The clock registers
- Fact: `JL_CLOCK` is at `0x00010000`: `PWR_CON` +0, `SYS_DIV` +8,
  `CLK_CON0` +12, `CLK_CON1` +16, `CLK_CON2` +20, `CLK_CON3` +24. In
  `CLK_CON0`: bit 0 turns the RC oscillator on and bit 1 picks its rate
  (0: 250 kHz, 1: 16 MHz); bits 4-5 pick the oscillator input (0: the
  crystal oscillator, the SDK's "BT OSC"; 2: the RTC's low-frequency
  oscillator; 3: a pad); bits 6-8 pick the main (system) clock source:
  0 the RC oscillator, 4 the crystal oscillator, 6 the RTC's low-frequency
  oscillator, 7 the PLL. In `CLK_CON1`: bits 2-3 the DAC clock (0: PLL
  24 MHz, 1: oscillator, 2: low-speed bus clock, 3: off); bits 10-11 the
  UART clock (0: oscillator, 1: PLL 48 MHz, 2: low-speed bus clock, 3:
  off). The SDK's definitions of the PLL's control fields and of `SYS_DIV`'s
  fields are switched off in its header (they may belong to another chip),
  so they are not given here (Q-2). In fwtest none of these registers has
  an effect (HW-11), and `SYS_DIV` bit 3 releases core 1 (HW-10).
- Sources: SDK `WL82.h` lines 15-16, 347-358 (`JL_CLOCK`); SDK
  `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/clock_hw.h` lines 235-341 (the fields in
  use) and 344 (the PLL and `SYS_DIV` fields under `#if 0`).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: real hardware (Level 2)

### HW-54: System clock rates, and FM-1's own setting
- Fact: On the chip, the SDK sets the system clock anywhere from 24 MHz to
  396 MHz, and names the rates 320, 240, 192, 160, 120, 96, 48, 40, 24, 12
  and 8 MHz. The high-speed bus clock is the system PLL clock divided by 1
  to 4, and the low-speed bus clock that divided again by 1 to 8; the SDRAM
  clock runs from 96 MHz to 244 MHz. FM-1's own firmware runs the PLL from
  the 24 MHz reference (HW-11) to 240 MHz. It tells a 24 MHz reference
  from a 40 MHz one by bits 26-27 of the word at `0x000119A0`
  (`JL_ANA->PLL_CON0`): the value 2 means 40 MHz, any other 24 MHz; the
  FM-1 takes the 24 MHz path. fwtest runs at 240 MHz from the start
  (HW-11), the rate FM-1's own firmware sets.
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/clock.h` lines 44-55 (the
  named rates), 94 and 97 (24 MHz to 396 MHz; SDRAM 96 MHz to 244 MHz),
  109 (the bus clock dividers); SDK `WL82.h` lines 488-546 (`JL_ANA` at
  `0x00011900`, `PLL_CON0` its word 0x28); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §5.1
  (the PLL from 24 MHz to 240 MHz, high confidence) and §5.2 (the
  reference detect, the 24 MHz path on the FM-1).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE)
- Needed by: real hardware (Level 2)

content.content:
## The raw image

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Format | A flat binary: the bytes of the code window, from its first byte. No header, no ELF. |
| Load address | The image's first byte is at `0x02000000`, the start of the code window. Link it there. |
| Entry | Core 0 starts at `0x02000000`: the image's first instruction. |
| Size | 1 byte to 1 032 192 bytes (1 MiB less 16 KiB). |
| The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. |
| Past the image | Reads in the code window after the image's last byte show the flash chip: window address `0x02000000 + n` shows chip offset `0x4000 + n`. Changes the image makes to the chip (erase, program) show through the window, also over the image's own bytes. |
| Writes to the window | Ignored (and listed as unmodelled accesses). |
| RAM | 1 MiB at `0x01C00000`, all zero at the start. Other memories, and what the real chip has: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| Core 0 at the start | User mode. Every register is 0, both stack pointers included (set your own stacks first), except `r0` = `0x01C7FC00`: a 64-byte block of zeros whose first word holds `0x01C7FC40`. |
| Core 1 | Does not run until the image releases it (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md` says how). Then it runs alongside core 0. |

## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.
What happens instead (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-52, says it with the measured
values):

- Misaligned loads and stores complete. A word load or store uses the 4
  bytes at the address given; a halfword load from an odd RAM address
  ignores the lowest address bit.
- Reads outside every memory and register fwtest models give 0, writes
  there are dropped, and both are listed in `unmodelled_accesses`; so are
  writes to the code window, which are dropped too.
- A division by zero gives 0.
- An instruction fwtest cannot decode ends the run as a fault (exit 3).
  fwtest may stop at the start of the straight-line code that holds it,
  before any of that code has run, and `result.json` then gives that
  address as the fault's `pc`; to have code run up to it, put the
  instruction behind a call or a branch.
- A jump outside every memory runs what fwtest reads there (zeros) for up to
  1024 instructions, until fwtest next checks the program counter, and then
  ends the run as a fault.

for them.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.
What happens instead (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-52, says it with the measured
values):

- Misaligned loads and stores complete. A word load or store uses the 4
  bytes at the address given; a halfword load from an odd RAM address
  ignores the lowest address bit.
- Reads outside every memory and register fwtest models give 0, writes
  there are dropped, and both are listed in `unmodelled_accesses`; so are
  writes to the code window, which are dropped too.
- A division by zero gives 0.
- An instruction fwtest cannot decode ends the run as a fault (exit 3).
  fwtest may stop at the start of the straight-line code that holds it,
  before any of that code has run, and `result.json` then gives that
  address as the fault's `pc`; to have code run up to it, put the
  instruction behind a call or a branch.
- A jump outside every memory runs what fwtest reads there (zeros) for up to
  1024 instructions, until fwtest next checks the program counter, and then
  ends the run as a fault.

### HW-20: Enabling a source, and its priority
- Fact: Each core has its own enable and priority words, `ICFG00` to
  `ICFG31`: core 0's at `0x01EEF100` to `0x01EEF17C`, core 1's at
  `0x01EEF300` to `0x01EEF37C`. Source n uses 4 bits of word n / 8, at bit
  position 4 × (n mod 8): bit 0 enables it, bits 1-3 are its priority 0-7.
  A higher number is a higher priority. A source interrupts only the cores
  whose words enable it.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214, 280-312; SDK `hwi.h` line 135
  ("0~7, larger is higher"); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §4.1 (the 4-bit
  encoding and the two arrays); E-3, E-9 (sources enabled this way).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-21: The global interrupt gates
- Fact: A core takes interrupts only while both gates are open: bit 8 of
  its special register `icfg` (the master enable; not to be confused with
  the `ICFG00`-`ICFG31` words of HW-20) and the enable set by the
  instruction `sti` (cleared by `cli`). At entry `icfg` reads 0, so bit 8
  is clear: set it and execute `sti` before expecting interrupts.
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/irq.h` lines 19-21 (bit 8
  of `icfg` as the enable); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §4.1, §5.2; E-1
  (`icfg` 0 at entry); E-3 (interrupts taken after setting `icfg` bit 8
  and executing `sti`).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-22: Entering and leaving a handler, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, when a core takes an interrupt the address to return to
  is put in the special register `reti` and the core jumps to the handler;
  the handler returns with `rti`. A handler compiled with the toolchain's
  interrupt function attribute returns correctly. A running handler can be
  interrupted by a pending source of higher priority only after it has
  stored `reti` to its stack, and only until it loads `reti` back; sources
  of the same or lower priority wait until it returns. When several enabled
  sources are pending, the one with the highest priority is taken; between
  equal priorities the order is not specified. fwtest models only core 0's
  tick timer and software-interrupt words (HW-17, HW-23), and one vector
  table for both cores. Whether the chip behaves the same way is Q-10.
- Sources: the emulator model; E-3 and E-9 show only that handlers written
  with the toolchain's interrupt attribute run repeatedly and return.
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M1

### HW-23: Software interrupts
- Fact: Writing bit b (0-7) to `ILAT_SET` makes source 120 + b pending;
  writing bit b to `ILAT_CLR` clears it. Core 0's are at `0x01EEF1A0` and
  `0x01EEF1A4`, core 1's `0x200` higher (fwtest has core 0's only, HW-22).
  The handler must clear its source, or it is taken again on return.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214, 322-323; SDK `cpu.h` line 59 (the
  SDK raises one this way); E-3: `ILAT_SET` bit 0 ran the handler of
  source 120 once, which cleared it.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-24: Waiting for an interrupt, in fwtest
### HW-17: The core tick timer
- Fact: Each core has a tick timer, `TTMR_CON`, `TTMR_CNT`, `TTMR_PRD`:
  core 0's at `0x01EEF0EC`, `0x01EEF0F0`, `0x01EEF0F4`, core 1's `0x200`
  higher (`0x01EEF2EC` ...). Its interrupt source is 3. In fwtest (core 0's
  only, HW-22), `TTMR_CON` bit 0 runs it, bit 7 reads 1 while its interrupt
  is pending, and writing bit 6 acknowledges it (write bit 0 as well to
  keep it running); it fires every 10 ms whatever `TTMR_PRD` holds. On the
  chip the period comes from `TTMR_PRD` (Q-4).
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214 (one block per core, `0x200`
  apart), 274-276; SDK `hwi.h` line 41 (`IRQ_TICK_TMR_IDX` 3); E-3: with
  `TTMR_PRD` = 1234 it interrupted every 10 ms (5 by 52.3 ms),
  acknowledged as above.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

## Open questions

What isn't known, or is known only from material the spec may not use. A
spec request can turn one into a fact.

sec='''## 14. Floating point and the second core (SR-5, SR-6)

### HW-62: The core's CPU model, and hardware single-precision float
- Fact: JieLi builds the SDK's AC791N code for the toolchain's CPU model
  `r3` with its hardware single-precision float extension `fprev1`:
  clang's `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`, and for link-time optimisation the linker
  plugin's `mcpu=r3` and `-mattr=+fprev1`. So the vendor's own code for
  this chip uses the extension's instructions, and each core reports five
  float conditions in `EMU_MSG` (bits 16 to 20, HW-50). Build firmware for
  the chip with `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`, as the SDK does. What `r1` to `r5`
  differ in, and how the extension behaves at its edges and in cycles on
  the chip, the sources don't say (Q-16).
- Sources: SDK `apps/demo/demo_hello/board/wl82/Makefile` lines 73-75
  (`-mcpu=r3`, `-mfprev1`), 233 and 273-274 (the linker plugin's
  `mcpu=r3`, `-mattr=+fprev1`); SDK `csfr.h` lines 267-272 and SDK
  `cpu/wl82/debug.c` lines 70-110 (the float bits of `EMU_MSG`, HW-50).
  The sources are the vendor's build settings and register map; no
  datasheet states it.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: M5 (SR-5)

### HW-63: Floating point in fwtest
- Fact: fwtest executes the `fprev1` instructions (add, subtract,
  multiply, divide, min, max, multiply-add and multiply-subtract, the
  conversions between float and signed or unsigned integer, and the float
  compares) on the ordinary registers, as IEEE 754 single precision:
  - results rounded to nearest, ties to even, with subnormals kept (no
    flush to zero); a division by zero gives an infinity of the right sign;
  - multiply-add and multiply-subtract round the product before the add
    (not fused);
  - a conversion to integer truncates toward zero and saturates at the
    integer type's limits; a NaN converts to 0;
  - min and max with one NaN operand give the other operand;
  - ordered compares are false when either operand is a NaN, their
    unordered negations true.
  No float condition sets an `EMU_MSG` bit or raises source 1 (HW-52).
  Each of these instructions is one instruction and one cycle, like every
  other (HW-11); fwtest models no extra cost for divide, square root (a
  library call, not an instruction) or conversions. Whether the chip
  rounds, keeps subnormals and treats NaNs the same way, and its cycle
  costs, is open (Q-16).
- Sources: the emulator model; HARNESS ("Time").
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M5 (SR-5)

### HW-64: The two cores in fwtest: pace, memory and interrupts
- Fact: In fwtest, once released (HW-9), core 1 executes one instruction
  per cycle at 240 MHz like core 0 (HW-11). The cores take turns: core 0
  runs 1024 instructions, then core 1 runs as many cycles as passed. They
  share one memory with no caches, no bus or memory contention and no
  wait states, so neither core slows the other, and a store by one core
  is seen by the other core's next load; but because of the turns, the
  other core sees it up to one turn (1024 cycles, about 4.3 µs) later.
  `testset` is atomic between the cores and `csync` has no effect. Core 1
  takes interrupts: the sources its own `ICFG` words enable (HW-20, from
  `0x01EEF300`), behind its own gates (HW-21), through the one vector table
  (HW-18, HW-22). The tick timer and software-interrupt words are core
  0's only (HW-17, HW-23): a source pending there interrupts every core
  whose `ICFG` words enable it, so enable each source on one core only.
  When core 1 loops with nothing changing (a polling loop), fwtest ends
  its turn early; its instruction counts are kept per turn (HARNESS,
  `ipb.csv`).
- Sources: the emulator model; HARNESS ("The raw image", "Outputs").
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M5 (SR-6)

### HW-65: Sharing memory between the cores, on the chip
- Fact: On the chip, the SDK's lock between the two cores is a byte taken
  with the atomic test-and-set instruction `testset` (repeated while the
  byte was already set), with `csync` before and after; it is released by
  `csync` and then a plain store of 0. Its atomic read executes `csync`
  before the load. The chip has instruction and data caches with shared
  controls (`CACHE_CON`, `DCACHE_WAY`, `ICACHE_WAY` in the `corex2` block,
  words 2 to 4 from `0x01EEE000`); the SDK flushes and invalidates data
  cache lines by address range, and divides the data cache's ways between
  the cores and the peripherals. Its uncached-address macro gives an
  address at or above `0x04000000` an uncached alias `0x04000000` higher,
  and returns lower addresses, main RAM's included (HW-6), unchanged. So
  for data shared between the cores, follow the SDK: `testset` for locks,
  `csync` before a shared load and around a lock. Whether main RAM is
  behind the data cache, and whether a plain store is seen by the other
  core's load without `csync`, the sources don't say (Q-18).
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/cpu.h` lines 49-50 (the
  uncached alias), 134-148 (`csync`, the atomic read), 189-190 (the

  invalidate, the way split); SDK `csfr.h` lines 106-118 (`corex2`).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: M5 (SR-6)

content.text:
All three requests are answered in PR #63, and its CI passes. SR-4 is answered in full; SR-5 and SR-6 are answered in part, with open questions where the sources don't settle things.

**SR-4**
1. **Audit:** Plaits is base code only for `firmware/demos/plaits/`, as you chose.
   - Those files get their own JPlag pass, and the text check uses the same base code.
   - A core file that includes a Plaits header fails the audit with a message telling the owner to decide.
   - The local self-test finds all 15 of our files. With a trial demo file it found 16 of 16.
2. **Separation check:** the firmware side should keep #59's version (#59 is now merged).
   - I found one gap: `vendor/plaits/SOURCE.md` is our own text but wasn't scanned. #63 scans it now; it has no hits.
   - R-SEP-1 and R-AUDIT-4 are amended.
3. **#59's branch:** the check passes, with no hits.

**Your note on universal constants:** powers of two, 2^n−1, 2^n+1, sign-bit masks and the standard IEEE 754 constants are no longer counted as emulator terms. The set is defined by rule in code, with tests both ways, and R-SEP-1 is amended. On #61's branch:
- Under #61's current copy of the check: 25 hits. That is #61's only failing CI check.
- Under the new rule: it passes, with no hits.

**SR-5 (floating point):**
- The SDK builds all its AC791N code with `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1` (this chip's CPU model plus its hardware float instructions); I checked 9 of its build files. The firmware side should build for the chip the same way.
- In fwtest, float results follow IEEE single precision, and every float instruction costs one cycle. No float condition raises an exception or sets a flag.
- Open: the chip's cycle costs and its edge-case behaviour (Q-16). fwtest's float timings should be treated as a best case.

**SR-6 (the second core):**
- In fwtest:
  - Both cores run at the same rate, with no caches and neither slowing the other, so the measured 0.50–0.55 is a best case.
  - Core 1 takes its own interrupts.
  - A store by one core reaches the other within 1024 cycles.
- On the chip, the SDK's practice is an atomic test-and-set (`testset`) for locks and a `csync` around memory shared between the cores; the firmware side should do the same.
- Open: core 1's clock, contention between the cores, its start-up needs, and whether main RAM is cached (Q-17, Q-18).

**What didn't happen:**
- Docker stopped responding after the disk filled. So I built no new black-box experiments, and the fwtest facts in SR-5 and SR-6 are marked emulator-only.
- No fwtest change was needed: no source shows different behaviour.
- The disk now has 5.6 GB free, and my scratch files are deleted.

**Merge order**
1. **#63** now.
2. **#61** after it merges main. Its separation check then passes. Expect small conflicts where both PRs add lines to PROVENANCE.md, EXPOSURE.md and REQUIREMENTS.md. I used P-31 because #61 already takes P-29 and P-30.
